client: I've been really stressed out about this networking event coming up next week — just thinking about it makes my heart race and my chest feel tight. I'm supposed to walk in there and introduce myself to all these people in my field, and I just freeze up even imagining it. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to make that feeling go away, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: What you're describing — that racing heart, the tightness in your chest, the mental freeze — sounds really overwhelming, and I can hear in the pace and tension of your voice that this is genuinely weighing on you right now. It takes courage to show up here and talk about it even when you're not sure it'll help, and that instinct to try anyway is actually a really meaningful first step. Let's gently explore what thoughts are driving that freeze response, because often the anxiety isn't about the event itself, but about a specific story our mind is telling us about what *could* go wrong there.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I mean... I guess that makes sense, the idea that it's a story my mind is telling. But honestly, it doesn't feel like a story — it feels completely real, like I genuinely know something bad is going to happen at this work presentation next week. The thought that keeps coming up is that I'm going to blank out in front of everyone and they'll all see that I don't actually know what I'm talking about, and then it'll just... confirm what I already suspect about myself.
therapist: That fear feels absolutely real and immediate — and the way you're speaking, with that urgency and tension, tells me this thought about blanking out and being "found out" carries a lot of weight for you. What you're describing sounds like it might connect to something deeper, almost like you're waiting for this event to confirm a verdict you've already quietly reached about yourself — and that's worth slowing down and gently examining. What is it exactly that you suspect about yourself, if you're willing to share that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... if I'm being honest, I think I'm waiting for people to realize I'm not as competent as they think I am. Like there's this version of me that everyone sees at work, and then there's the real me who's just kind of fumbling through everything and hoping no one notices. And the presentation feels like the moment the curtain finally gets pulled back.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, almost carefully, like you were admitting something you've been holding privately for a long time — really comes through, and I want you to know it takes real courage to name that. What you're describing has a name: it's called impostor syndrome, and it's remarkably common among people who are actually quite capable — the fumbling you feel on the inside often doesn't match the competence others genuinely see on the outside. I'd love to gently challenge this with you: what actual evidence do you have that the "real you" is an impostor, versus evidence that you've earned your place there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I've heard of impostor syndrome before, and honestly, part of me wonders if that label is just... a convenient way to explain away something that might actually be true about me. Like, what if I really am just not as good as people think, and the label is just making me feel better about a real problem? When you ask for evidence, my mind immediately goes to all the times I've stumbled in meetings or said something that didn't land right — that feels more real to me than any success I've had.
therapist: The speed and intensity in your voice right now tells me this fear feels very urgent and convincing in this moment — and I want to gently point out something important: your mind is doing something called *selective attention*, where it's collecting every stumble as iron-clad proof while almost automatically discarding your successes as flukes or luck. That's not your mind being accurate — that's your mind being *biased*, and we can actually test that bias: if a close colleague described your work performance, would they only remember the moments you stumbled, or would they see a fuller, more balanced picture than the one you're painting of yourself right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I mean... I guess a colleague probably wouldn't describe me the way I describe myself, but that almost makes it worse somehow, like maybe they just don't see what I see. Maybe I'm the only one who knows how close I am to falling apart on the inside, and they're just seeing this surface version of me that's holding it together. It feels less like bias and more like I have access to information they don't.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, at a higher pitch, like the words are trying to keep up with your thoughts — tells me this idea feels very urgent and certain to you, even as the words themselves carry a kind of quiet resignation. But I want to gently offer a reframe: what you're calling "insider information" is actually your experience of your own anxiety and self-doubt, which is *not* the same thing as objective truth about your competence — everyone has an internal world that feels messy and precarious, and that internal chaos doesn't cancel out the real, visible impact you have on the people around you. The question worth sitting with is: could it be that both things are true — that you *do* struggle internally sometimes, *and* that you are genuinely capable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it feels almost too convenient, like you're just trying to make me feel better rather than actually engaging with the reality of my situation. The anxiety and self-doubt aren't random noise to me — they feel like they're tracking something real, like my brain is picking up on signals that I'm not as capable as people think I am. And honestly, the idea that both things can be true at the same time just sounds like a way to avoid the harder question of which one is actually right.
therapist: The tension and speed in your voice right now tells me this isn't just an intellectual debate for you — this feels urgent and personal, like something really important is at stake, and I want you to know I'm not trying to talk you out of your reality or make you feel better with empty reassurance. You're actually asking a really sharp question, so let's take it seriously: if your anxiety were a perfectly accurate detector of incompetence, we'd expect it to show up *only* when you're actually performing poorly — but does it? Or does it show up even when things go well, even when you're prepared, even when others respond positively to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, okay, that's... that's actually a fair point, and I hate that it is. Because honestly, the anxiety shows up the most when I'm about to present something I've actually worked really hard on, something I know inside and out, and it's still there screaming at me that I'm going to fall apart. But I guess part of me still wants to argue that maybe it's just... being cautious, like it's trying to protect me from getting too confident and then failing.
therapist: The way you said "I hate that it is" — softly, quickly, almost like you were catching yourself — tells me something just shifted a little, like a part of you recognized something true even though it's uncomfortable to sit with. What you're describing about the anxiety showing up *most* when you're most prepared is actually really significant evidence against the idea that it's tracking reality accurately — a genuinely protective signal would quiet down when you're well-prepared, not get louder. And that reframe of it being "cautious" is worth holding gently: it might be your mind trying to stay safe, but there's a difference between a system that protects you and one that's become so sensitive it goes off even when there's no real threat.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me does get it logically. But it's hard to just... accept that the anxiety is lying to me, because in the moment it feels so real and so urgent, like if I ignore it something will actually go wrong. I guess I'm worried that if I start dismissing it, I'll miss something important and then it'll be my fault when things fall apart.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, at a high pitch, even as the words themselves feel heavy and resigned — tells me this fear of "missing something important" feels both urgent and exhausting to carry. I want to name something important here: you're not being asked to *ignore* the anxiety or pretend it isn't there — in CBT we're not trying to silence it, but to stop giving it *veto power* over what you know to be true. The goal is to be able to hear that alarm going off and say "I notice you, and I'm going to check the actual evidence before I act on you" — because that's very different from dismissing it, and it keeps you in the driver's seat rather than letting the anxiety steer.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it — like, intellectually it makes sense that I don't have to just obey the anxiety. But in the moment when I'm, say, refreshing my work email at midnight because I'm terrified I missed something critical, it doesn't feel like a choice I'm making — it feels like I genuinely have no option but to check. How am I supposed to pause and "evaluate evidence" when my brain is already convinced the worst is happening?
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, softly, at a high pitch, like you're describing something that happens *to* you rather than something you do — really captures how trapped that midnight email-checking feels, and I want to acknowledge that the compulsion feels completely involuntary in that moment. What you're describing is actually the anxiety's most powerful trick: it creates such urgency that the checking feels like the *only* logical response, but each time you check, you're actually teaching your brain that the threat was real and the checking kept you safe — which makes the next urge even stronger. So the goal isn't to pause and philosophize at midnight — it's to start building small moments of *delay* during lower-stakes moments, so that gradually your brain learns it can tolerate the uncertainty without the check, and that nothing catastrophic actually happens.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets the logic of it — like, intellectually I can see how checking might be making things worse. But when you say "start with lower-stakes moments," I honestly can't think of what those even look like, because every email feels high-stakes to me, even during the day. What if I delay and something actually does go wrong, and then it's my fault for not catching it in time?
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now, even as the words themselves feel almost resigned, tells me this fear of being "at fault" is carrying enormous weight — like every email has become a potential verdict on your responsibility as a person. I want to gently name what's happening here: your mind has quietly expanded the stakes of *everything* until there's no such thing as a low-stakes moment, which is actually the anxiety protecting its own survival — because if everything is urgent, you can never safely practice letting go. So the real question worth sitting with isn't "what if something goes wrong?" — it's "how many times have you actually missed something critical during the times you *didn't* check immediately, versus how many times has the urgency turned out to be your anxiety rather than a real emergency?"
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
